extracted.intended_audience: government cost analysts, Navy HRM managers, and contracting/financial analysts performing OMB A-76 in-house vs contract cost comparisons
extracted.subtask_short: OMB A-76 cost_comparison for IT services
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter from an academic thesis that applies OMB Circular No. A-76 cost-comparison framework to evaluate whether the HRMIN human-resources information service should remain in-house or be contracted out (timesharing/service bureau). Includes detailed cost-element definitions, measurement methods, benchmarking/adjustment procedures, and qualitative benefits/disadvantages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect time (vendor charge factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Connect time to the computer--the duration of an active transmission link between the user's terminal and the timesharing system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendors may base charges on connect time. In benchmarking and contract cost development, connect time is a primary driver of charges and is adjusted to reflect 'real' usage (see adjustment factor example dividing benchmark hours by in-house hours). Connect time is assumed functional (not learner errors) for adjustment purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: CPU time / Processing (vendor charge factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: CPU time [Processing] -- the period a program occupies the central processing unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendors may charge for CPU time separately from connect time. The analysis assumes processing time is on average directly proportional to connect time when adjusting vendor benchmarks to in-house profiles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage capacity (vendor charge factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Storage capacity--required for the user's programs or data files.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On-line storage requirements should be set (example: three years of data used in the benchmark) and assumed unchanged unless justified otherwise. Storage-related charges (e.g., surcharges) are included in contract cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel time / I/O requests (vendor charge factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel time--the duration of channel use sometimes measured by counting the number of I/O requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Channel time can be a separate billing metric and should be measured or estimated when benchmarking vendor quotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional charges (vendor charge factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional charges -- may be made for file access, languages, applications programs, and terminal and communication equipment rentals. [Ex: SPSS royalty fees]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include software royalties, language or application surcharges, terminal/communication rentals when comparing contract quotes. Example: SPSS royalties were a specific other direct cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of contracting out (timesharing) - fewer programming errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Fewer programming errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a potential benefit of contracting to a computer service organization; benefits are intangible and often difficult to quantify but should be recorded when comparing alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of contracting out (timesharing) - no training required
rubrics_metrics.description: No training required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendor-provided services can reduce in-house training needs; quantify avoided training costs where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of contracting out (timesharing) - known costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Known costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracting can convert uncertain in-house costs into fixed/known contract prices; include contract administration and other added charges when treating costs as 'known.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of contracting out (timesharing) - no equipment maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: No equipment maintenance (and other logistic support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoided maintenance and logistics are benefits; if vendor retains responsibility for maintenance, estimate the avoided maintenance expense in the cost comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of contracting out (timesharing) - minimum personnel problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimum personnel problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracting can reduce HR/personnel management issues; these qualitative effects should be noted though they may be hard to monetize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of contracting out (timesharing) - increased future capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Increased experience and capability for future expanded efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendors may bring broader experience that can benefit future projects; capture as qualitative benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits of contracting out (timesharing) - greater workload handling capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater capability for handling varying workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vendors may scale more readily; include degree of scalability in qualitative assessment and sensitivity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantage: expensive for some users / limited terminal speed issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Timesharing is needlessly expensive for users who do not benefit from quick responses or who have a high volume of transactions. Most keyboard terminals have limited speeds, which increase communications charges if there is much data transmission. Although remote batch processing reduces these charges, it increases turnaround time to minutes or hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume timesharing is always cost-effective—evaluate user needs (response time, transaction volume) and terminal capabilities; consider remote batch processing trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantage: timesharing introduces considerable overhead
rubrics_metrics.description: Timesharing introduces considerable overhead that users must ultimately pay for. The split-second choreography required for multiple users necessitates a costly operating system. Communications costs may also be considerable versus on-site I/O. When timesharing is vended by an outside commercial firm there are added charges to cover marketing, administration, taxes and profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include vendor overhead/loadings and commercial margins when comparing to in-house costs; consider hidden administrative/marketing taxes and profit components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantage: usage delays and technical hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Usage can be delayed from minutes to hours because of telephone line or computer difficulties. In general, timesharing systems are relatively sophisticated with the resultant hazard of technical problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include potential downtime, communication failures, and their operational impacts in qualitative risk assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantage: data security problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Data security problems are accentuated by timesharing. Retrieving list data may be difficult because of systems' dynamic interactions. The user must therefore consider safeguarding all programs and data with copies. Similarly the vendor should install software and access procedures that prohibit unauthorized trespassing on others' property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess vendor security measures, data segregation, and backup procedures; quantify potential costs of breaches or additional security controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Labor (cost element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct Labor
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct labor is a basic cost element and should be accumulated using representative operational positions rather than prorated part-year labor. The thesis used assumed operational positions (see Part D) to compute a 'real' direct labor cost; compare both prorated actuals and representative operational estimates. All labor was considered direct for operations overhead purposes in this analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fringe Benefits on Labor (cost element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fringe Benefits on Labor
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accumulate fringe benefits based on employee categories (e.g., permanent GS employees not subject to FICA or premium holiday pay but eligible for retirement). Use actual fiscal-year data where available (example: FY82 fringe $31,357.55).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations Overhead (cost element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations Overhead
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operations overhead consists of many sub-elements (indirect labor; indirect materials and supplies; depreciation; rent; maintenance and repair; support costs; utilities; insurance). Each sub-element should be examined individually and either measured or allocated (some items are aggregated into G&A). Use representative operational-year estimates (example maintenance moved from FY82 $34k to FY84 estimate $40k).

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Direct Costs (cost element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other Direct Costs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This element contains sub-elements such as software royalties (example SPSS royalty), travel, training, and telecommunications. Telecommunications may have significant fixed (e.g., ~$2,000/month) and variable components (example variable ~$1,500 for November 1982), driving sensitivity of in-house costs to utilization. Aggregate and disclose sensitivity (example doubling usage increases yearly cost ~ $18,000).

rubrics_metrics.name: General and Administrative Expenses (G & A) (cost element)
rubrics_metrics.description: General and Administrative Expenses
rubrics_metrics.guidance: G&A is charged from a central pool to cost centers and broken down by job order. Use actual cost center allocations (example Code 205 and Code 16) and aggregate to total G&A for the base year (example FY82 total $31,487).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inflation (cost element treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inflation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inflation is not germane to a base-year cost comparison. When analyzing only a single base year for an already-running system, exclude inflation unless comparing multi-year projections or out-year differences between alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of Capital / Opportunity Cost (cost element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost of Capital
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate opportunity cost of capital using net book value of assets and an assumed opportunity-cost rate (example: net book value $227,848 and opportunity cost rate 10% producing $22,785). Include this to capture the capital tied up in the performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: One-Time and Other Costs (cost element treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: One-Time and Other Costs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One-time and other costs are not appropriate when assessing an existing in-house performance in a base-year comparison because the system is already running; exclude unless analyzing conversion or transition scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations Overhead sub-element: Indirect Labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect Labor
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervision and user training may be considered direct labor in some analyses; for this study supervision by the manager and training of users were considered direct labor supporting the service, and indirect labor was aggregated into G&A. Define clearly what counts as direct vs indirect labor for consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations Overhead sub-element: Indirect Materials and Supplies
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect Materials and Supplies
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operating supplies (computer paper, pens, clips) may be aggregated into G&A or allocated by cost center; provide cost-center-level breakout where possible (example: Code 205 $2,930; Code 16 $5,132; total $8,062 applied to HRMIN).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations Overhead sub-element: Depreciation (straight-line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Depreciation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use straight-line depreciation to spread tangible capital asset cost over estimated useful life (example: assumed 5-year useful life). For base-year comparisons of an already-owned system, treat capital costs as sunk and exclude acquisition cost if assets are already government-owned. Example depreciation amounts: HARRIS computer $54,814/year; disk drives $9,360/year; terminals $12,232/year; total $76,406 (FY82).

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations Overhead sub-element: Rent
rubrics_metrics.description: Rent
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rent may be accounted for in aggregate G&A; if relevant, allocate actual rent charges to the cost center rather than omitting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations Overhead sub-element: Maintenance and Repair
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance and Repair
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use maintenance contract rates or estimates for an operational system (example FY82 $34,000; estimate FY84 $40,000 used to be more representative). Prefer operational-year estimates over single-year anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations Overhead sub-element: Support Costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Support Costs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounted for in G&A aggregate unless separable; include support functions required to operate the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations Overhead sub-element: Utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilities
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utilities may be aggregated into G&A; if material, estimate usage-related utility costs attributable to the operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operations Overhead sub-element: Insurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If government is self-insured, calculate insurance factor appropriately (example: insurance factor = .0006 x total producing $112/year in the thesis). Document method and apply consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depreciation / sunk cost treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: For the purpose of this cost comparison their costs are sunk costs and not considered because by the time of publication of this work all of this capital will be owned by the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assets are already government-owned, treat acquisition costs as sunk and exclude them from the base-year in-house cost comparison; still show depreciation and book values for transparency and to compute insurance or cost-of-capital where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Direct Costs sub-elements (SPSS royalty, travel, training, telecom)
rubrics_metrics.description: SPSS royalty, travel expenses, training costs, telecommunications services (telecom fixed + variable costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List and quantify each sub-element; example values—SPSS royalty rose from $2,500 (FY82) to $3,500; travel $1,950; training $8,000; telecommunications ~$3,500/month representative ($42,000/year). Flag telecom as highly user-sensitive and include sensitivity analysis (doubling use increases yearly in-house cost by about $18,000).

rubrics_metrics.name: General & Administrative allocation practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The G & A expense pool at NPRDC charges a portion of the pool to each cost center and is broken down by job order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use actual cost-center G&A allocations (examples: Code 205 $17,268; Code 16 $14,219; total FY82 G&A $31,487). Document allocation basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmarking vendor quotes using representative jobs
rubrics_metrics.description: The benchmark package consisted of three 'typical' SPSS programs supplied by NPRDC. The benchmark was conducted in 1980 to estimate expected utilization and to benchmark respondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you cannot fully benchmark vendors yourself, adjust published or third-party benchmark quotes using representative in-house jobs (supply sample programs used in the benchmark). Ensure benchmarks reflect realistic on-line storage and utilization assumptions; document any discounts or assumptions applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: User profile determination / usage measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine user profile using job accounting features (HARRIS job accounting) and remote access records (Tymnet) to measure connect time and CPU usage. Example: sum of allocated time 1,598 hours 20 minutes (host), CPU time 223 hours 47 minutes, ratio connect:CPU = 7.14:1. 'Real' yearly connect time postulated = 4,740.5 hours for base year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available logs for a representative period (example Sept–Dec 1982 and Tymnet Nov–Dec 1982). Do not assume future increases unless explicitly included; for base-year comparison, use measured base-year usage. Document period and methodology for extrapolation to yearly values (e.g., working days * average daily hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment factor to scale vendor benchmark to in-house usage
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjustment factor calculated by dividing vendor benchmark hours (derived from vendor price divided by an assumed $/hour rate) by postulated in-house yearly connect time to scale connect time and processing charges (example Tymshare: $219,120 / $16/hr = 13,695 benchmark hours; 13,695 / 4,740 = 2.9 adjustment factor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the adjustment factor to vendor connect-time and processing-time charges to reflect actual in-house usage. The example uses a 'worst case' $/hour rate to produce a conservative (smallest) adjustment factor; state clearly assumptions for the hourly rate used. If vendor hourly rate differs, adjust accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption: processing time proportional to connect time
rubrics_metrics.description: The last assumption necessary to consider is that processing time is directly proportional to connect time on the average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use proportionality assumption cautiously; validate with measured CPU:connect ratios where possible. If the job mix varies greatly, proportionality may not hold and you should separate CPU and connect components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmark representativeness and sensitivity disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Postulation of a 'real' FY82 HRMIN user profile was done by assuming the representativeness of available user data. The benchmarked costs were adjusted using factor 2.9; that is, Tymnet calculated 2.9 times too much connect time in their benchmark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When relying on benchmarks or limited measurement periods, document representativeness, the adjustment factor, and sensitivity of conclusions to key assumptions (e.g., connect-time, telecom usage). Recommend re-running the study when a longer historical usage pattern is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular No. A-76 low-bid rule and early-stopping heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB Circular No. A-76 requires the 'low bid' be used when conducting a cost comparison. When the basic contract price exceeds the total in-house costs it can be assumed that the cost of in-house performance will be less than the cost of contracting-out; this precludes the necessity for completing portions of the comparison dealing with the cost of contracting-out, except for certain exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the lowest contract price > total in-house cost, you may stop further contract-cost detail work because the conclusion won't change; however, still consider potential federal income taxes and proceeds from disposal of assets as possible offsets, and add contract administration costs (example: 4%) when comparing final prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions / offsets to the OMB early-stopping rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The only exception to the above is the consideration of potential federal income taxes, and proceeds from disposal of assets. Also consider the cost of administering the contract (example 4%) added to the basic price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the low bid exceeds in-house cost, test whether tax implications or asset disposal proceeds could materially change the conclusion. Explicitly add contract administration percentage to contract price to compare to in-house cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calculate total in-house performance cost by summing cost elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Total In-House Performance Cost is the sum of direct labor, fringe benefits, operations overhead, other direct costs, general & administrative expenses, and cost of capital (example total $383,505.00 for FY82).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present a table of accumulated costs by element (as done in Table 4). Use actual FY data where possible and justified estimation procedures where not. Provide comparison table to lowest-cost contract-out alternative and show cost differential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity analysis and recommendation to re-evaluate with longer data
rubrics_metrics.description: It is recommended that this study be repeated when a historical usage pattern for HRMIN is documented (after about five years) and sooner if industry capabilities and costs change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend periodic re-evaluation and perform sensitivity analysis (e.g., doubling telecom use increases in-house cost by ~ $18k). Note that technology and vendor market changes may shorten the recommended re-evaluation interval.
